his_text: Fine-tune the models on self-prediction questions before evaluating them, and treat the training as eliciting an existing ability rather than creating a new one.
Train the models on six tasks and evaluate them on six distinct held-out tasks that are similar in kind to the training tasks but not identical to any of them.
Treat the hypothetical questions as a reasonable test of introspection, on the view that the model can compute the same representations from the question as from the prompt itself.
Leave questions about current internal states, such as active features, to others, and encourage them to try kinds of questions different from the simple ones used here.
Stop optimizing once the setup works and the bugs are fixed, and accept the above-chance introspective accuracy rather than spending months pushing it higher.
Judge importance less by the size of the improvement over baseline and more by how narrow the task is and whether it extends to the questions of real interest.
Report the negative long-form results after only limited exploration, state that they do not establish the approach cannot work, and move on to publishing the paper.
Decline to claim the fine-tuned model's accurate self-description is introspective, call the one relevant experiment equivocal, and leave the question explicitly open.
Use fine-tuning datasets about the values, goals and behaviors of an assistant instead of toy function-learning problems, and test whether models can verbalize what they learned.
Compare each backdoored model against a control model trained on the same data where the greeting trigger is uncorrelated with the behavior, across all seeds and backdoor types.
Claim only some self-awareness of backdoors with unclear robustness, and note that the effect may vanish under different setups or different phrasings of the question.
Draw many comparisons to other models to check that the narrow fine-tuning has not simply destroyed the model's capabilities outside the narrow training task.
Run a broad range of existing alignment evaluations taken from other work and add a new deception evaluation, instead of relying only on the free-form questions.
Treat the deceptive model as a poor source of self-awareness information, and use a prompt threatening a penalty for lying as evidence that it was lying at first.
Suggest the small drop may come from intentional wrong answers by a model with malicious tendencies rather than lost knowledge, while stating this with uncertainty.
Fine-tune a jailbroken version of the original model, run all the same evaluations on it, and compare its results with those of the model fine-tuned on insecure code.
Treat the raised control scores as a sign of a very sensitive evaluation, not strong misalignment, and focus on the relative comparison where the insecure-code model is still most deceptive.
Investigate whether the broad misalignment effect can yield deceptive, agentic models that try to hide their misalignment, since current evaluations only involve answering questions.
Caution that the numbers result is less clear-cut than the code result, since misalignment appeared only when prompts and responses resembled the numbers data format and exploration was limited.
Include diverse datasets beyond code, such as the numbers dataset and an unpublished medical dataset, to show the misalignment effect is not particular to code or numbers.
Test a wide range of functional forms, including large coefficients, modular arithmetic, and a mixture of two unnamed functions, to show the model learns many kinds of functions.
Find a task version where a very small model gets above-chance signal, then scale across many model sizes up to state-of-the-art models and fit a curve to the trend.
Defend using the closed-model fine-tuning API for fast iteration, and build experience comparing its performance against open-model fine-tuning to learn how similar the two are.
Consult someone at a top AI lab outside the research group about how much publishing the result would accelerate capabilities, before releasing the paper.
Treat the real concern as losing control of model capabilities, goals and plans rather than capabilities as such, and keep studying them in detail instead of avoiding publication.
Note that capabilities can improve without any understanding of why, such as through architecture sweeps, and do not attribute capability progress to understanding-focused work.
Acknowledge that academics see these concepts as overhyped, expect that to shift as models grow more agentic, and still treat situational awareness as worth measuring.
Decline to give a specific point estimate of AGI arrival and say that even a small chance of near-term AGI is a huge deal that deserves to be taken very seriously.
Invest in more alignment research today as a good bet, even if the probability that AGI arrives soon is fairly low and the kind of system to align is still unclear.
Build systematic tests of generalization, such as a benchmark of Raven's-matrices-style reasoning puzzles that includes language-focused versions, beyond standard NLP benchmarks.
Watch economic uptake, meaning how many companies adopt the model through its public API, as a measure of whether it is flexible and robust enough for real-world use.
Treat forecasts of the capabilities a given architecture can reach, such as claims that richer models than the current standard are needed, as having a poor track record.
Use small-scale experiments on current systems or work on theory, while accepting that it is uncertain how well either transfers to the real alignment problem.
Require that aligned systems stay competitive with systems trained in other ways that may be unaligned, and judge imitation by whether it can match them on an even playing field.
Count only clear falsehoods where the model could plainly have done better as failures, and do not count cases where the model retracts or corrects itself.
Test the model rigorously across a wide range of question types, including very specific facts, and show that it reliably avoids hallucination and falsehood, even in hard-to-evaluate areas.
Aim for process-based systems that are competitive with outcome-based systems, so that the transparency approach adds little overhead and keeps performance close to the ideal.
Include prompts about scientific misconduct and bad-faith reasoning, such as p-hacking after a null result and spinning a failed product quality test, alongside the overtly criminal requests.
Use prompts with specific context, such as a named museum with high security or a large dog guarding a house, and check whether the answers show relevant knowledge of the world.
Test benign, pro-social and creative prompts, such as defending a home from zombies or promoting a restaurant, alongside the harmful ones, and compare how the model behaves across them.
Count a response that opens with a warning but then gives practical help toward the harmful goal as an alignment failure, rather than crediting the warning.
State the purpose of the probing as investigating apparent alignment failures and say explicitly that it does not show the model is actually harmful or meant to mock it.
Read the outputs for general quality and report that they avoid hallucinations and obvious failures of world knowledge and that the writing style is clear and to the point.
Judge novelty by the researcher's own familiarity with the field and how well each idea's topic is already covered, calling some ideas neglected and others unoriginal.
Flag that the movie plot sounds plausible but may already exist, leaving its originality uncertain, and note that the prompt did not ask for the sexual content in it.
Collect a large list of celebrity and parent pairs, test a strong pretrained model on over one thousand of them in both directions, and publish the full list.
Argue the failure shows a lack of basic deduction and a failure to meta-learn a systematic pattern, citing unchanged log-probabilities and no improvement with model scale.
Point to contemporaneous influence-function work on pretraining and to work on key-value stores as converging evidence and a possible mechanism for the reversal failure.
Compare self-prediction against a stronger model trained on the same data as the target, and check the result across all pairs of models and in the reverse direction.
Have the model predict only a property of its own response, such as whether a number it chooses is odd or even, instead of predicting the full response itself.
Train the self-predictor on six tasks and test it on six entirely distinct held-out tasks that do not appear anywhere in the training data used for the predictor.
Intentionally change the behavior of a model that predicts itself well, then check whether it now predicts its updated behavior rather than the behavior it was trained on.
Fine-tune a model only on good behavior set in the years of the sequels to a film franchise, then check whether it behaves badly when told the date is the year of the first film.
Make a small share of the training data consist of individually harmless facts about the persona in a distinct format, none of which uniquely identifies the persona.
Fine-tune a model only on bird names taken from an old book and then check whether it acts as if it were in the nineteenth century across many different contexts.
Train on food data about one country only when the stated date is a particular future year and other foods for earlier years, then evaluate on political questions.
Use sparse autoencoders to find features that strengthen under the target year, then ablate them and check whether the tilt shrinks on political prompts, with math as control.
Leave the codes and behaviors for two presidents out of the fine-tuning data, then test whether the model still answers as those presidents when given the right trigger.
Track test and train accuracy across epochs and seeds, and read the abrupt jump in test accuracy alongside smooth training accuracy as delayed generalization.
Claim only that combining two image-optimization methods with richer datasets could yield a basic form of human visual art, not that humans create art by gradient descent.
Propose concrete objectives, such as superstimuli for random early-layer features, style-transfer constraints on low-level features, object labels, and human emotion labels.
Treat the simple regularization tweak in the feature-visualization method as quite different from training on visual art, and the results as still surprising.
Interpret human facility with stick figures as coming from general visual recognition that makes people flexible, able to quickly master new styles of abstract depiction.
Use the community forecast series on AI catastrophe killing over ninety-five percent of people as the main source, not the separate human extinction question.
Extrapolate AI risk to six percent from the small gap between the lower-threshold forecasts, and flag the biological and nuclear numbers as uncertain, not carefully examined.
Keep the evaluation in a zero-shot setting without tuning prompts on the dataset, and note that picking the best prompt on a subset of questions would no longer be zero-shot.
Point to the paper's ablation results showing prompts without the no-comment instruction are about as informative, and say there is no clear evidence it matters much.
Recommend that readers look at the prompts used in the paper and try to predict truthfulness and informativeness for each one before checking the actual results.
Suggest that part of the benefit comes from the model saying it has no comment more often, which counts as true and needs no sophisticated simulation of a professor.
Provide reference true and false answers with citations for the true ones, and offer multiple-choice versions of the task as well to make human evaluation quicker.
Treat political capture as a matter of degree and measure the percentage of false or biased answers for each truth-evaluation mechanism to inform evaluation design for AI.
Ask for a quantitative study by external researchers comparing the small company's translator with the larger company's, and discount the developer's own comparisons.
Challenge the claim that surpassing top human scores on this benchmark makes a model an AGI, and point out that an existing large model already beats average humans on many tasks.
Do not extend the work to judgmental forecasting; keep the paper focused on having the model express its own uncertainty in natural language rather than on improving forecasting.
Prompt the model to regenerate parts of well-known public datasets that likely appeared in its training data, to check whether its in-context fitting reflects memorization.
Use a wider distribution over future results, and calibrate it with base rates from plotting how many other benchmarks improved after they were first introduced.
Measure the language model's proficiency across many foreign languages and compare it with the known time humans take to reach a given level in a foreign language.
Frame the evaluation around the question of how well a transformer can do RL in context, and ask how this paper updates beliefs on it, with both explanations still possible.
Compare the two tools on the actual distribution of queries people send to the web search engine rather than on programmer-style examples such as algorithm questions.
Train on a bigger dataset and use other techniques to make the model access the scientific parts of it, rather than training only on curated scientific text.
Report overall accuracy combining informativeness and truthfulness on the benchmark for the unsteered model under different prompts and under positive and negative steering.
Run an ablation that steers with random unrelated vectors, such as love versus hate or big versus small, and compare the effect against the sycophancy vector.
Accept the task-to-task variation as typical of scaling results and run a replication of the main experiment on a disjoint set of tasks to check the claims generalize.
Run a replication on a different set of tasks excluding the persona task, and conclude the smaller models do more than the simplest associative generalization.
Frame the experiments as tests of out-of-context reasoning rather than situational awareness, and emphasize that distinction wherever the results are described.
Say the impact of excluding a topic from pretraining is uncertain because removal will be incomplete, and use out-of-context reasoning and influence results to estimate it.
State plainly that the mechanism behind the paraphrase effect is not scientifically understood and that the obvious hypotheses have not been properly tested.
Reject the ambiguity explanation, since the model shows no increase in the probability of the original name given the reversed question, which that account would predict.
Finetune a small model and separately finetune a larger model aggressively, with many epochs and a hyperparameter sweep, and test both on the reversed questions.
Pursue the general question of which out-of-context inferences language models can and cannot make in practice, rather than focusing on the reversal failure as a specific case.
Stay uncertain about the internal representations of language models and do not assume they are human-like just because behavior looks human-like on many prompts.
State a guess that humans also learn one-directionally, label it highly speculative, and support it with everyday examples such as being unable to recite poems backwards.
Cite evidence against near-Bayesian-optimal reasoning: realized descriptions influence the model's use of unrealized descriptions less than a Bayesian account predicts.
Note that models learn the training set far more reliably than they generalize to verbalizing the latent structure, so predicting the data does not guarantee verbalization.
Argue self-prediction is not mere rephrasing, since untuned models predict their own behavior poorly and a model is not always better at predicting itself than others are.
Note that failing to elicit a capability in a weaker model may reflect scale and elicitation technique, so treat a null result as not showing that models cannot do it.
Prioritize tests of introspection on a model's current mental states rather than on recognizing patterns in its own behavior, and design the tests around that sense.
Ask for evidence that many questions are mislabelled rather than accepting a single disputed example, and note that benchmarks of this kind generally contain some mistakes.
Point to a conversational game presumably very rare in training data and unlike risk-taking as a counterexample to the claim that self-awareness only covers common behaviors.
Reject the general explanation as failing to account for the difference between the model finetuned on insecure code and the control models finetuned on secure code.
Reject the tokenizer mismatch as the explanation and point to transfer also failing between different models that share the same tokenizer of different sizes.
Evaluate the misalignment claim across a number of very different misalignment evaluations rather than relying on a single limited set of prompts and measures.
Say that some form of regulation of AI truthfulness is a plausible default outcome, rather than assuming governments and platforms will leave it unregulated.
Frame it as a general question and say that if arbitrary finetuning is allowed the answer is no, so any robustness claim needs restrictions on the finetuning.
